Doesn't the EPA shut down private companies that do this? What are we, the people, going to get from them destroying our land?

Info on the spill from the State of Colorado: https://www.colorado.gov/pacific/cdphe/animas-river-spill

The link above also has links to EPA's website, State of New Mexico, and a local health department.

Here is a link to data on the spill from EPA: http://epaosc.org/site/doc_list.aspx?site_id=11082

The highest concentration of copper measured in the Cement Creek (tributary to the Animas River, I believe) was a little over 2,000 ug/L or 2.000 mg/L. That concentration dropped to less than half of that amount in about 12 hours.

To add some perspective here, there is something called the EPA Multi-Sector General Permit. It is a basic permit that authorizes industrial facilities, mines, and other entities to discharge stormwater from their sites into surface waters such as rivers. It applies in only a handful of states, including New Mexico but not including Colorado (the other states would have their own versions of the permit). In any event, if there were an active metal mining facility in the State of New Mexico that was covered by this permit, they would have to meet benchmark concentrations for various metal parameters in the stormwater going into the surface waters. The facility would not be in violation of the permit if the stormwater discharged from their site exceeded the benchmark concentrations, but they would have to perform additional actions and could I suppose face fines if they did not take adequate steps to improve the discharge from their site.

For copper, the benchmark concentration varies between 0.0038 and 0.0332 mg/L depending on the conditions of the receiving water. These values are about 2 to 3 orders of magnitude less than the highest concentration measured in the river. Mind you, the benchmark is what you are allowed to put into the receiving water, not the expected values in the receiving water themselves! To be fair, the baseline average at the particular location I'm referencing is 0.07393 mg/L, which is above benchmark values anyway.

For other metals sampled, the maximum benchmark for zinc is 0.260 mg/L. At the Bakers Bridge location in the Animas River, the maximum value looks to be about 1.7.

Of course, this data is from August 5 and 6. Conditions could be better or worse at this point.

Tl;dr The concentration of some metals measured in the Animas River and Cement Creek are greater than what is allowed to be discharged in stormwater leaving active metal mining sites in New Mexico.
